methods.label: Count the parity patterns
methods.explanation:
Only the parities of the four integers matter. From \(0\) through \(2007\), there are \(1004\) even numbers and \(1004\) odd numbers. Since the choices are independent, the \(2^4=16\) parity patterns are equally likely.

For either ordered pair \((a,d)\) or \((b,c)\), write \(E\) for even and \(O\) for odd. Its four patterns are \(EE,EO,OE,OO\). Only \(OO\) gives an odd product; the other three give an even product.

The difference \(ad-bc\) is even exactly when the two products have the same parity. Both products are odd in \(1\cdot1=1\) pattern, and both are even in \(3\cdot3=9\) patterns. These cases are disjoint and include every even difference. Hence
\[
\Pr(ad-bc\text{ is even})
=\frac{1+9}{16}=\frac58.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\frac58}\), choice E.
methods.levelReason: The solution reduces the experiment to four binary parity choices and counts them using elementary addition and multiplication.

candidate.annotationRationale: Parity and equally likely probability are the task targets. The method enumerates parity patterns, then combines disjoint cases with multiplication and addition. Equal parity counts and independent sampling justify assigning each pattern the same probability.

review.mathematicalCheck: There are 1004 integers of each parity. Independence makes all 16 parity patterns equally likely. Matching product parities occur in \(1+9=10\) patterns, so the probability is \(10/16=5/8\).
